source.title: Beyond Occam's Razor in System Identification: Double-Descent when Modeling Dynamics
source.authors: Antônio H. Ribeiro; J. Hendriks; A. Wills; Thomas Bo Schön

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Extends the double-descent investigation to nonlinear system-identification models and dynamic-system datasets, with experiments sweeping model capacity and measuring test error.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier deep-network and other double-descent results but does not test deep networks. Rows below concern its own capacity sweeps and reported test-error outcomes. The neural-network discussion is a theoretical connection and reports no new neural-network test-error results.
record.test_reason: It runs its own capacity sweeps (random Fourier features, RBF features, random-forest leaves) on dynamical-system data and reports test MSE past the interpolation threshold. This bears on V4 in a new setting, and a ridge-strength comparison bears partly on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors show double descent appears in nonlinear ARX system identification, on synthetic and real (CE8) data. They present minimum-norm solutions and ensembles as mechanisms producing the second descent, and note that smaller ridge λ makes it more explicit.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use nonlinear ARX and related system-identification models, including RFF, RBF, and random forests, rather than deep-network scaling experiments. They vary features or leaves and measure prediction MSE on dynamical-system data; some overparameterized solutions use ensembles.
record.method_sensitivity: For RFF models, the prominence of double descent changes with ridge-regularization strength: it is more explicit for smaller lambda values.

fits_no_version.finding: For minimum-norm RFF solutions, the parameter norm peaks at the interpolation threshold and then decreases monotonically as features grow.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The minimum-norm parameter norm peaks at interpolation and falls with further overparameterization, accompanying the second descent.

record.peer_reviewed: IFAC-PapersOnLine; the text says the preprint will appear in the Proceedings of the 19th IFAC Symposium in System Identification.
record.problems: Most reported test-error curves are presented in figures without numerical values in the supplied text. The explicit error-bar information applies to the Figure 2 repetitions; comparable uncertainty details are not stated for the other experiments. Noise variation, sample-size variation, and training-time sweeps are not performed.

untested.parts: No deep-network size sweep. Neural networks get only a theoretical (linearization / gradient-descent min-norm) connection.
No sweep over epochs or training time.
Training sample size is fixed (T=400 or T=3000). No sample-size sweep.
No effective-complexity measure is tested for predicting the peak across axes.
Label noise is not varied, there is no triple or multiple descent, and optimally tuned regularization is not tested.
There is no re-parameterisation of complexity by an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: All results are figure-only; no numerical test errors appear in the text. Uncertainty bands (interquartile range over 10 runs) are given only for Fig. 2. The second descent beyond the threshold depends on how the solution is selected (min-norm or ensembles). A possible further V4 scope point is that free-run training error reaches zero only at m/T greater than 1, but the test curve still shows the second descent. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks are discussed and cited, but no deep-network model-size sweep is performed.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
Training sample count is held constant in the reported capacity sweeps; no near-threshold sample-size increase is tested.
Tests capacity-related test-error curves in system-identification models, not every model class or setting.
Parameter norm is plotted against model size, but the study does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
Tests the effect of ridge-regularization strength on the curve. Does not vary noise, test for triple or multiple descent, or test optimally tuned regularization.
Does not test whether an appropriate effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.reason: Test MSE shows a classical U-shape, a peak at m/T≈1, then a second descent beyond interpolation, for both one-step-ahead and free-run MSE (r1, r2, r5, r6, r7, r8, r9, r10). The evidence is figures plus qualitative text only.

relationships.reason: Larger λ makes the double-descent peak less explicit, and the curve approaches the min-norm curve as λ→0. This is directionally consistent with regularization suppressing the peak, but complete disappearance under optimal λ is not shown (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Increasing λ made the peak less pronounced, while letting λ approach zero recovered the minimum-norm curve.
